props.title: Ferrari: Race to Immortality

sections.content: **Ferrari: Race to Immortality (2017)** (2017) plunges into Formula 1's deadliest era, when Enzo Ferrari's ruthless pursuit of victory in the 1950s claimed multiple drivers' lives. This raw documentary shares DNA with Rush (2013) and **Grand Prix** (1966), but strips away Hollywood gloss to expose the brutal reality of early F1. Through restored footage and haunting interviews, we follow Ferrari drivers Peter Collins and Luigi Musso as they chase glory at 170mph in paper-thin cars. The film captures an era when racing meant dancing with death every weekend.

sections.content: Racing documentaries hit different when they capture the sport's raw danger. **TT: Closer to the Edge** (2011) follows modern Isle of Man racers still risking everything, while **1: Life on the Limit** (2013) chronicles F1's evolution from deadly spectacle to high-tech showcase. But none match Ferrari's 1950s crucible, where young racers faced mortality in primitive machines. Director Daryl Goodrich weaves restored footage into a haunting tribute to an era when the prancing horse logo often meant a dance with death.

The film's genius lies in humanizing these forgotten heroes. Through intimate interviews and private footage, Collins and Musso emerge as vibrant young men, not just statistics. Like **Weekend of a Champion** (1972), which captured Jackie Stewart at his peak, it reveals racers as complex humans. The restored 1950s racing footage, meanwhile, carries the visceral punch of **Grand Prix** (1966), minus any Hollywood sanitization. SUBHEAD: The Human Cost of Speed

sections.content: Enzo Ferrari's complicated legacy anchors the narrative. Like Howard Hughes in **The Aviator** (2004), his genius came with a dark side - a willingness to sacrifice young men for victory. The film doesn't judge but presents stark facts: 15 Ferrari F1 drivers died in the 1950s. This makes modern racing docs like **Williams** (2017) feel almost tame by comparison. When today's drivers bemoan safety features, **Ferrari: Race to Immortality** serves as a sobering reminder of racing's blood-soaked roots.
